intro: A stately little procession in three beats, with trills on its repeated notes and sudden runs up the keyboard. Marcelle Meyer plays Scarlatti’s E-major sonata on the piano.

sections.label: A · Repeated notes and trills
sections.mNote: Three-beat phrases travel from E major to B major

sections.label: A · The procession starts again
sections.mNote: The first half repeats from E major

sections.label: B · A new phrase over B
sections.mNote: The second half begins in the dominant key

sections.label: B · The return to E repeated
sections.mNote: The second half retraces its route to E major

cues.title: Three trills in a row
cues.text: The opening phrase steps down, then answers with three repeated notes, each carrying a trill. Scarlatti keeps the three-beat measure plainly in view. The hands take turns with the little descending figure before the runs begin.
cues.evidence: Scarlatti, Sonata K. 380, piano edition reproduced as IMSLP 691879, bars 1–12. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Singing for the queen
cues.text: Scarlatti arrives in Lisbon on 29 November 1719. At the palace he sings while Queen Maria Anna accompanies him. His new pupils include her daughter Maria Bárbara, whose service will eventually take him to Spain.
cues.evidence: Cristina Fernandes, Scarlatti, Giuseppe Domenico, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 91 (2018), citing the papal nuncio’s account of Scarlatti’s arrival. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: The opening steps return
cues.text: The first half has reached B major, a fifth above the home key. The repeat brings back E major and the descending phrase with its three trills. The first few bars leave the lower hand silent while the upper hand speaks.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, first repeat at bar 40, returning to bars 1–4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Art’s ingenious play
cues.text: In the address to the reader of his Essercizi, published in 1738, Scarlatti offers “art’s ingenious play” to develop fluency at the harpsichord. His invitation welcomes amateurs and professionals alike.
cues.evidence: Our translation of “lo scherzo ingegnoso dell’arte” from Scarlatti’s address to the reader, Essercizi per gravicembalo (London, 1738), quoted by Cristina Fernandes: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/.

cues.title: A phrase over B
cues.text: The second half begins in B major, where the first half ended. The left hand supplies repeated bass notes while the right hand shapes a new phrase. The music still moves in three; this time its destination is E major.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, bars 41–44 and the E-major ending. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second half again
cues.text: After reaching E major, the piano returns to the start of the second half. The familiar repeated notes and quick decorations retrace their route. The ending brings a falling run, a trill and the last E in the bass.
cues.evidence: Piano edition, second-half repeat and final bars, ending at bar 78. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B major returns to E
transitions.how: A descending run and trill bring the first half to B major. The repeat restores the opening E-major phrase in the right hand, leaving the left hand silent for four bars. Its three repeated trills announce the restart.
transitions.evidence: Piano edition, bars 39–40 followed by bars 1–4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf

transitions.title: The B bass stays
transitions.to: B · A new phrase over B
transitions.how: The first half closes in B major, and the second half keeps that key for its new phrase. The left hand moves from the held cadential bass into repeated notes; above it, the right hand mixes short repeated notes with a rising run.

transitions.title: E major reopens onto B
transitions.from: B · A new phrase over B
transitions.to: B · The return to E repeated
transitions.how: The final descending run settles on E, with the same note low in the bass. Taking the repeat restores the second half’s B-major opening. The held ending is followed by the left hand’s regular three-beat accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Piano edition, bars 77–78 and return to bar 41. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both recording sources identify Meyer; the chronology identifies the Scarlatti piano session. No historical keyboard type is inferred from the composition’s age.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano performance of the keyboard sonata
fields.note: A single complete sonata is hosted, not a movement from a multi-movement set. The date 1754 is retained as a Venice-manuscript copy date, not a proven composition date. Meyer’s edition and editorial interventions are unknown. The Longo reference score’s fingering, dynamics and other editorial directions are not attributed to Scarlatti or to Meyer. The two repeated halves are mapped provisionally from the score and audio report, not a note-by-note alignment.

fields.note: Restoration, equalisation, noise reduction, edits and speed correction are undocumented. The analysis’s global B-major estimate is not proof of transposition, mistuning or a wrong file; the score’s key is E major and local estimates include E near the close.

US public-domain status is not established and is not asserted; Commons also carries its pre-1972 US-recording copyright warning. The generic public-domain metadata and composition-only tag are not the sound-recording clearance. No first-publication date is invented from November 1954.

composer.epithet: A royal teacher whose sonatas send the hands flying across the keyboard, then bring them together for a song.
facts: Alessandro Scarlatti’s sixth child; born in 1685, the year of Bach and Handel
Maria Bárbara of Portugal, later Queen of Spain; he served her until his death
Naples and Rome; Lisbon from 1719; Spain from 1729
555 in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; most survive in manuscript copies
composer.background:
Alessandro Scarlatti had an eagle to launch. Writing to Ferdinando de’ Medici on 30 May 1705, he described his nineteen-year-old son Domenico: “This son is an eagle whose wings have grown; he must not idle in the nest, and I must not prevent his flight.” The boy already had a post as organist at the royal chapel in Naples and operas to his name. His father sent him north towards Venice, by way of Florence, with a recommendation that could hardly be improved upon. Domenico would eventually settle much farther from home, teaching a Portuguese princess whose marriage took them both to Spain.

Born in Naples on 26 October 1685, the same year as J. S. Bach and Handel, Domenico was the sixth of Alessandro’s ten children. His family included singers as well as composers; opera was a family business. He became a salaried royal organist at fifteen. Rome gave him another kind of court: Maria Casimira, the widowed Queen of Poland, maintained a theatre in her Palazzo Zuccari. Scarlatti supplied her with seven operas between 1710 and 1714, working with the poet Carlo Sigismondo Capece and the stage designer Filippo Juvarra. There were words, costumes and human voices in his working life long before it became a matter of sonata numbers.
